\chapter{How Far Away}
\label{ch:ml-distance}
\hlchaptermodality{81}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say that something is near or far, and ask how far away it is.}

From cold: both ends of the distance scale, the question that reads it, and the difference between pointing at a place and measuring across to it.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[aṭuttŭ]{\ml{അടുത്ത്} (aṭuttŭ) — near}

\label{lesson:ML-C81-aduthu}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{here}. Say \emph{there}. Then think about what neither of them tells you: \textbf{how far away.}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{അടുത്ത്}}
\textbf{\ml{അടുത്ത്}} — \emph{aṭuttŭ} — near, close by.

\textbf{\ml{ഇവിടെ}} and \textbf{\ml{അവിടെ}} \emph{point}. They split the world in two — where I am, and where I am not — and that is all they do. Something \emph{aviṭe} might be across the room or across an ocean, and the word is the same either way.

\textbf{\ml{അടുത്ത്} measures.} It is the first word in this track that says \textbf{how much space is involved} rather than which side of you it is on.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{does} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{ഇവിടെ} / \ml{അവിടെ}} & \textbf{point} — this side or that \\
\textbf{\ml{അടുത്ത്}} & \textbf{measure} — not much space \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

That is a real division, and it is the reason a learner can have owned \emph{here} and \emph{there} for forty chapters and still be unable to say that the shop is close.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The near end of a scale you could previously only point along.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{aṭuttŭ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{iviṭe}, then \emph{aṭuttŭ}, and say which of the two told you a distance
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{aṭuttŭ} mean? (\textbf{Near, close by}.) And what can it tell you that \emph{aviṭe} cannot? (\textbf{How far away something is}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[akale]{\ml{അകലെ} (akale) — far away}

\label{lesson:ML-C81-akale}



\begin{quote}
Say the word for \emph{near}. Then say the three-way pattern the pointing words are built on.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{അകലെ}}
\textbf{\ml{അകലെ}} — \emph{akale} — far away.

The scale now has both ends:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{അടുത്ത്}} \emph{aṭuttŭ} & near \\
\textbf{\ml{അകലെ}} \emph{akale} & far \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Between them you can place anything, and \textbf{\ml{അവിടെ}} stops having to do a job it was never built for.

\begin{culture}
Look at \textbf{\ml{അകലെ}} and \textbf{\ml{അവിടെ}} side by side. Both open with \textbf{\ml{അ}}, and the pointing pattern you learned says that \textbf{\ml{അ}-} is the \emph{away} one — \emph{aviṭe}, \emph{that place}, over there.

\textbf{Resist that.} The \textbf{\ml{അ}} in \emph{akale} is \textbf{part of the word}, not the pointing prefix stuck on the front of it. The pattern is real and this is not an instance of it; the two only look alike.

This is worth a page of its own because the habit it trains is the useful one. \textbf{A pattern you have learned will start finding matches everywhere, including where there are none.} The test is never how the word looks — it is whether the other members of the set exist. There is no \emph{ikale} meaning \emph{near} and no \emph{ekale} meaning \emph{how far}, so there is no set, so there is no pattern here.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{akale}
  \item \emph{aṭuttŭ}, then \emph{akale}
  \item why the \emph{a} at the front of \emph{akale} is not the pointing prefix
  \item what you would have to find for it to be one
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{akale}? (\textbf{Far away}.) What is its partner at the other end? (\emph{\textbf{aṭuttŭ}}.) And is its opening \emph{a} the pointing prefix? (\textbf{No — it is part of the word}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[etra dūraṁ]{\ml{എത്ര} \ml{ദൂരം} (etra dūraṁ) — how far}

\label{lesson:ML-C81-dooram}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{far away}. Then say the age question, the long one about what exists to you.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{ദൂരം}, and \ml{എത്ര} on its own}
\textbf{\ml{ദൂരം}} — \emph{dūraṁ} — distance.

\emph{aṭuttŭ} and \emph{akale} give you two rough settings. \textbf{\ml{ദൂരം}} is the thing itself — the amount of space, which can be asked for and answered with a number.

And you already own the word for asking. \textbf{\ml{എത്ര}} \emph{etra} — \emph{how much, how many} — has been sitting inside the age question since you learned it:

\textbf{\ml{നിങ്ങൾക്ക്} \ml{എത്ര} \ml{വയസ്സുണ്ട്}?} — \emph{to you, \textbf{how much} age exists?}

It was a piece of a phrase then. \textbf{Now take it out and use it.}

\textbf{\ml{എത്ര} \ml{ദൂരം}?} — \emph{etra dūraṁ?} — how much distance? How far?

That is the whole question, and it is two words you were given separately. \textbf{Lifting a word out of a phrase you already say is the cheapest vocabulary there is}, and it is worth going looking for: a long sentence you learned whole usually has two or three words in it that work on their own.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{അടുത്ത്}} & near — a setting \\
\textbf{\ml{അകലെ}} & far — a setting \\
\textbf{\ml{എത്ര} \ml{ദൂരം}?} & how far — a question with a number for an answer \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{dūraṁ} is a borrowing from Sanskrit, where \emph{akale} is inherited. Both are ordinary and neither is grander than the other; Malayalam keeps pairs like this all over, and having both is not a redundancy but a choice of texture.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{dūraṁ}
  \item \emph{etra dūraṁ?}
  \item the other question you know that starts with \emph{etra}
  \item \emph{aṭuttŭ}, \emph{akale}, \emph{etra dūraṁ} — two settings and the question
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{dūraṁ}? (\textbf{Distance}.) What does \emph{etra} mean on its own? (\textbf{How much, how many}.) And where had you already met it? (\textbf{Inside the age question}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[etra dūraṁ enna ōrmma]{(how far away) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ML-R81-distance-recall}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say \emph{near}, then say \emph{far}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: pointing and measuring are different jobs}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{job} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{ഇവിടെ} / \ml{അവിടെ}} & \textbf{point} — my side or not my side \\
\textbf{\ml{അടുത്ത്} / \ml{അകലെ}} & \textbf{measure} — a little space or a lot \\
\textbf{\ml{എത്ര} \ml{ദൂരം}?} & \textbf{ask} — and expect a number back \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The pointing pair had been yours for a long time and could not answer \emph{how far}, because splitting the world in two is not the same as measuring across it. Something \emph{aviṭe} can be a step away or a country away.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A scale, and the question that reads it.

One of the four words cost nothing. \textbf{\ml{എത്ര}} was already inside the age question you learned whole, doing exactly this job, and the chapter only took it out. \textbf{A long sentence you learned whole usually holds two or three words that work on their own} — worth going looking for, in this language and any other.

The chapter also asked you to \emph{refuse} a pattern. \textbf{\ml{അകലെ}} opens with \textbf{\ml{അ}} and the pointing prefix is \textbf{\ml{അ}-}, and they are not the same thing: there is no \emph{ikale} and no \emph{ekale}, so there is no set, so there is no pattern. \textbf{A pattern you have learned will find matches where there are none}, and the test is always whether the other members exist.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{aṭuttŭ}, then \emph{akale}
  \item \emph{etra dūraṁ?}
  \item which of your words point and which measure
  \item where \emph{etra} came from
  \item why \emph{akale} is not built on the pointing prefix
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which word means \emph{near}? (\emph{\textbf{aṭuttŭ}}.) Which means \emph{far}? (\emph{\textbf{akale}}.) And how do you ask for the number? (\emph{\textbf{etra dūraṁ?}})
\end{tcolorbox}
